An anatomical phantom exposes material bias in uncorrected amyloid-PET quantification

Across simulated gray-to-white matter ratios, uncorrected amyloid-PET measures had mean absolute inaccuracies of 14.1% for tissue ratio and 19.8% for SUVR; partial-volume correction reduced them as low as 6.1% and 7.6%, with modified 3-compartment and GTM methods performing best.

Key quantitative results: Uncorrected gray-to-white ratio and SUVR had mean absolute inaccuracies of 14.1% and 19.8%, respectively.

BiomarkersAmyloid PETAmyloid PET SUVRPET quantification

Added October 16, 2026 · DOI:10.1186/s40658-026-00956-3

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

Partial-volume effects can materially distort amyloid-PET SUVR, particularly when cortical atrophy or small structures mix gray and white matter signals. This phantom study shows that correction improves accuracy without a relevant loss of precision, but the best method still needs clinical validation on specific scanner, tracer and reconstruction combinations.

Study design

The StepBrain anatomical phantom was scanned to reproduce clinical amyloid-PET distributions across gray-to-white matter ratios from 0% to 120%. Atlas-based gray-to-white ratios and cerebellum-normalized SUVRs were calculated without correction and after 2-compartment, 3-compartment, modified 3-compartment and geometric transfer matrix correction. Linear mixed models compared accuracy and precision against the known phantom ground truth.

Key quantitative results

  • Uncorrected gray-to-white ratio and SUVR had mean absolute inaccuracies of 14.1% and 19.8%, respectively.
  • Partial-volume correction reduced mean absolute inaccuracy as low as 6.1% for gray-to-white ratio and 7.6% for SUVR.
  • Accuracy and precision differed significantly among methods for both measures (F>95 for all comparisons).
  • Three-compartment, modified 3-compartment and geometric transfer matrix correction improved tracer-ratio accuracy without relevant precision loss; modified 3-compartment and GTM were the most accurate and precise.

What changed

The study supplies a physical ground truth for comparing amyloid-PET partial-volume methods and quantifies how much uncorrected SUVR can be biased in clinically realistic uptake patterns.

Strength of evidence

Strong analytical-method evidence within a controlled phantom experiment, with direct ground truth and head-to-head methods. Clinical validity and utility remain unproven because a phantom cannot reproduce motion, biological heterogeneity, tracer kinetics, scanner diversity or patient-specific anatomy.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Quantitative amyloid-PET reports should identify whether and how partial-volume correction was applied, especially for longitudinal monitoring or low-burden decisions. The numerical results should not be used as a universal correction factor.

Field medical relevance

Useful for MSL and imaging discussions about SUVR bias, atrophy, longitudinal treatment monitoring, method harmonization and why quantitative pipelines require scanner- and tracer-specific validation.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The head-to-head phantom comparison provides a known ground truth for partial-volume bias. Modified 3-compartment and geometric transfer matrix approaches were most accurate and precise in this setup, but results do not establish universal equivalence across scanners, reconstructions, tracers, atlases or patient anatomy.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No access or coverage change. More advanced correction may require software, expertise and harmonized quality control that are not uniformly available.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Should every amyloid PET scan use the best-performing method from this study?
Not automatically. Modified 3-compartment and GTM performed best in this phantom, but each clinical pipeline needs validation for its tracer, scanner, reconstruction, atlas and patient population.
Does partial-volume correction eliminate bias?
No. It reduced mean absolute inaccuracy substantially but did not reduce it to zero.
Was clinical utility tested?
No. The study measured technical accuracy and precision, not diagnostic decisions, treatment selection or patient outcomes.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Phantom rather than patient data
  • Does not reproduce motion, biological heterogeneity or tracer kinetics
  • Single experimental imaging and processing setup
  • No clinical decision thresholds or outcomes
  • No authorization, guideline or coverage assessment
